60-prompt descriptive audit | English task audit

Numbered chapter-wise study roadmap

Each numbered topic below is a specific, independently answerable study task. Read its exact subquestions, open Ready-to-use AI prompt, then copy it into your AI agent. The prompt includes the subject, chapter, requested output, practice-answer requirements and source/date safeguards. You do not need to copy the entire chapter. Attach the linked notes when you want the agent to use those files; a different agent cannot automatically access files on this computer.

Static explanations, current source-verification tasks and applied practice are labelled separately. Current-topic prompts ask the agent to verify status; their presence here does not authenticate a latest figure or imply every subject requires monthly news. Task selection is a preparation recommendation, not a claim that every task appeared in a PYQ.

Print/PDF retains all numbered study tasks. The expandable prompt text and copy controls are HTML-only, avoiding hundreds of repetitions of the same output instructions in print.

Notes labels: Explained notes = authored Study Studio teaching prose; revision packet = maps/tables/cards without a complete teaching chapter; supplied PDF = your source notes, not a claim that all its contents have been freshly reviewed. Finance's October examples are not a complete static FM course and their dated claims still need verification. Where no explained chapter exists, that gap is explicit.

ESI 1. ESI Dictionary

1. Static topics: precise explanation and calculation tasks

  1. Static explanation
    GDP, GVA, GNI and NNI: choose the correct aggregate

    Define each aggregate and connect domestic/national, gross/net and market/basic-price valuation. Construct a numerical bridge using depreciation, net primary income from abroad and product taxes/subsidies; identify which adjustment changes which boundary.

    ESI / ESI Dictionary / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: GDP, GVA, GNI and NNI: choose the correct aggregate
    Link to this topic

  2. Static explanation
    Stocks, flows, rates and percentage points

    Classify public debt, fiscal deficit, wealth, saving, inflation and GDP growth. Use a hypothetical inflation change from 6% to 4% to calculate percentage-point and relative changes; explain why falling inflation is not falling prices.

    ESI / ESI Dictionary / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Stocks, flows, rates and percentage points
    Link to this topic

  3. Static explanation
    Liquidity, solvency, inclusion and welfare vocabulary

    Contrast a cash shortage with negative net worth, access with usage, and an income transfer with a public service. Give one banking and one household case where confusing the terms produces the wrong policy response.

    ESI / ESI Dictionary / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Liquidity, solvency, inclusion and welfare vocabulary
    Link to this topic

2. Current verification and chapter-specific application

  1. Current source verification
    Build a dated policy-term dictionary from one RBI statement

    Identify the most recent RBI monetary-policy statement you can verify. Extract repo, stance, operating target, liquidity and transmission in context; separate changed decisions from unchanged definitions and cite the statement date for each new fact.

    ESI / ESI Dictionary / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Build a dated policy-term dictionary from one RBI statement
    Link to this topic

  2. Current source verification
    Decode one Economic Survey paragraph without losing units

    Choose and cite a verified Survey paragraph on employment or growth. Explain every technical term, fiscal/reference year, denominator and estimate status; rewrite the paragraph in plain English without changing its statistical meaning.

    ESI / ESI Dictionary / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Decode one Economic Survey paragraph without losing units
    Link to this topic

Use the named-item evidence inventory to check historical questions. A chapter's presence here ensures breadth; it does not imply a separately observed question or guaranteed marks.

Additional connections to keep in view

  2. Fiscal/monetary, real/nominal and growth/development distinctions
  3. Banking, trade, welfare and demographic terms in application

  5. Record changed institutional or product definitions with effective dates

ESI 2. National Income Accounting

1. Static topics: precise explanation and calculation tasks

  1. Static explanation
    GDP at market prices versus GVA at basic prices

    Explain product taxes/subsidies versus production taxes/subsidies and derive the relevant GDP-GVA bridge. Solve an original numerical example; show why adding all taxes indiscriminately double-counts or misclassifies components.

    ESI / National Income Accounting / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: GDP at market prices versus GVA at basic prices
    Link to this topic

  2. Static explanation
    Nominal GDP, real GDP and the implicit deflator

    Calculate real and nominal growth and a GDP deflator from a consistent two-year dataset. Explain base-year effects, rebasing versus economic growth, and why the GDP deflator differs from CPI in coverage and weights.

    ESI / National Income Accounting / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Nominal GDP, real GDP and the implicit deflator
    Link to this topic

  3. Static explanation
    Expenditure GDP, inventories and welfare limits

    Construct GDP from consumption, investment, government final consumption and net exports without double-counting transfers or intermediate goods. Treat inventories and imports correctly; explain why rising per-capita GDP need not imply rising median welfare.

    ESI / National Income Accounting / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Expenditure GDP, inventories and welfare limits
    Link to this topic

2. Current verification and chapter-specific application

  1. Current source verification
    Read India's latest national-accounts release correctly

    Locate the latest verified MoSPI national-accounts release. Tabulate release date, GDP/GVA, nominal/real basis, fiscal period, base year and advance/provisional/revised status; reconcile one revision with an earlier release rather than treating it as new growth.

    ESI / National Income Accounting / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Read India's latest national-accounts release correctly
    Link to this topic

  2. Current source verification
    Compare RBI, IMF, World Bank and OECD growth forecasts

    Collect the latest verifiable India growth projections from those four institutions. Align calendar/fiscal years and forecast vintages, show revisions and stated drivers, and explicitly mark projections that are not comparable.

    ESI / National Income Accounting / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Compare RBI, IMF, World Bank and OECD growth forecasts
    Link to this topic

ESI 3. Economic Growth and Development

1. Static topics: precise explanation and calculation tasks

  1. Static explanation
    Growth versus development: when GDP is misleading

    Compare GDP growth with health, education, distribution and environmental outcomes. Explain three channels through which output can increase without broad welfare improvement; construct an assessment table rather than just defining development.

    ESI / Economic Growth and Development / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Growth versus development: when GDP is misleading
    Link to this topic

  2. Static explanation
    Capital accumulation, productivity and structural transformation

    Explain how capital deepening differs from productivity growth and how workers moving between sectors changes aggregate productivity. Use a small two-sector numerical example; discuss why labour movement may fail to create good jobs.

    ESI / Economic Growth and Development / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Capital accumulation, productivity and structural transformation
    Link to this topic

  3. Static explanation
    Inequality, poverty reduction and inclusive growth

    Explain how the growth rate, income distribution and access to public services jointly affect poverty. Compare redistribution with productivity-enhancing inclusion; evaluate one trade-off and one complementarity using hypothetical households.

    ESI / Economic Growth and Development / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Inequality, poverty reduction and inclusive growth
    Link to this topic

2. Current verification and chapter-specific application

  1. Current source verification
    WDR 2024: escaping the middle-income trap

    Verify the World Bank's 2024 report and explain investment, infusion and innovation as distinct stages. Translate the framework into constraints facing Indian firms; distinguish the report's recommendations from your own India-specific inference.

    ESI / Economic Growth and Development / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: WDR 2024: escaping the middle-income trap
    Link to this topic

  2. Current source verification
    Economic Survey growth constraints: evidence-to-policy map

    Use the latest verified Survey to identify three binding growth constraints. For each provide the cited evidence, causal mechanism, proposed intervention and implementation risk; do not substitute a list of growth forecasts for analysis.

    ESI / Economic Growth and Development / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Economic Survey growth constraints: evidence-to-policy map
    Link to this topic

ESI 4. School Of Economic Thoughts

1. Static topics: precise explanation and calculation tasks

  1. Static explanation
    Classical versus Keynesian response to deficient demand

    Compare assumptions about wage/price adjustment, involuntary unemployment, saving and investment. Analyse a recession with idle capacity and explain why demand stimulus has different effects when the economy is supply-constrained.

    ESI / School Of Economic Thoughts / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Classical versus Keynesian response to deficient demand
    Link to this topic

  2. Static explanation
    Market failure versus government failure

    Explain externalities, public goods, information asymmetry and coordination failure using Indian development examples. Match taxes, provision, regulation or information tools to each; analyse capture, administrative capacity and unintended incentives.

    ESI / School Of Economic Thoughts / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Market failure versus government failure
    Link to this topic

  3. Static explanation
    Inflation diagnosis before choosing a policy school

    Distinguish a demand boom, oil-price shock and monetary expansion. Compare likely output/price effects of fiscal tightening and monetary tightening in each case; avoid presenting one school as universally correct.

    ESI / School Of Economic Thoughts / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Inflation diagnosis before choosing a policy school
    Link to this topic

2. Current verification and chapter-specific application

  1. Applied practice
    Interpret one recent policy response through competing theories

    Select one verified Indian fiscal or monetary response to an economic shock. Explain the implicit assumptions, transmission and limitations from Keynesian and market-adjustment perspectives; separate observable evidence from theoretical interpretation.

    ESI / School Of Economic Thoughts / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Interpret one recent policy response through competing theories
    Link to this topic

  2. Applied practice
    Industrial policy: coordination support or rent protection?

    Construct a hypothetical production-incentive case. Explain the learning/coordination argument, fiscal and competition risks, sunset conditions and outcome indicators; show which evidence would distinguish capability building from permanent protection.

    ESI / School Of Economic Thoughts / Chapter notes and context

    Ready-to-use AI prompt: Industrial policy: coordination support or rent protection?
    Link to this topic

Topper interviews: tips, traps and practical decisions

Research checked 2026-11-12. Publisher-labelled cohorts 2022-2026; partial content review, not a complete playlist audit.

What was actually reviewed

357 playlist entries inventoried; 176 metadata records retrieved; 1 public transcript retrieved (selected preparation passages reviewed); 11 publisher-written profiles reviewed.

YouTube rate-limited the remaining metadata requests and further transcript access. This is not a claim to have watched every video. Written profiles are edited publisher accounts, not verified verbatim transcripts. Auto-captions can mishear names and technical terms. Year labels come from publisher titles/descriptions, not independently verified RBI selection records. Upload years are not selection years. Multiple clips from one person are not independent endorsements.

The 2026 evidence uses Divyanshu's timestamped transcript passages; 2025 uses Raghav Manglik's written profile; 2024 uses Ankit Pandey, Satender Singh and Tanay Gaurav; 2023 uses Sai Gireesh, Prashant Meena and Tejdeepthi; 2022 uses Utkarsh Agrawal, Prasanth Akkiraju and Shobhita Bhola. Bhavana P J is supplemental evidence with no independently established cohort here.

All findings are paraphrased. Practical actions and safeguards below are our synthesis, not topper quotations or official RBI prescriptions.

The preparation loop to remember

  1. Learn the exact demand.
  2. Recall without notes.
  3. Apply, calculate or type.
  4. Diagnose the error.
  5. Repair and retest on fresh material.

357-entry coverage inventory | Evidence data and sources | Standalone readable report

18 actionable tips and corresponding traps

Phase I

1. Protect every sectional gate; do not abandon your strengths

What the accessible sources report

  • He describes earlier sectional failures, overconfidence after a previous clearance, and the cost of shifting all attention to a weak subject while neglecting stronger ones. Divyanshu (name as transcribed) at 13:50.
  • Her written profile describes clearing the overall threshold but failing Quant in an earlier attempt, followed by better question selection. Shobhita Bhola (written summary).
  • His profile attributes a later Phase I failure to overconfidence and stopping mocks despite earlier interview-stage progress. Satender Singh (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

Track the score, accuracy, time loss and recurring error types for each section separately. Maintain a practice slot for stronger sections while repairing the weakest gate. Set your own practice buffer from current official requirements and varied mocks; past cutoffs are not safe targets.

Trap: A good aggregate, an earlier Phase II clearance, or being an engineer does not guarantee this year's sectional clearance.

Phase I / execution

2. A mock is useful only when the next attempt changes

What the accessible sources report

  • He describes alternating mocks with analysis of speed, accidental correct answers, learnable weaknesses and topics not worth rescuing under his remaining time. Divyanshu (name as transcribed) at 30:40.
  • His profile describes a dedicated error notebook and attempting to avoid those same mistakes in subsequent mocks. S. B. Tanay Gaurav (written summary).
  • His profile describes returning to concepts when mock analysis exposed a weak topic. Ankit Pandey (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

For wrong, guessed-right and slow questions, record the cause: concept, recall, calculation, interpretation, question selection or time. Write a corrective task, then use a fresh timed question to test the repair. Re-solving a familiar item can train a procedure but does not prove transfer to unseen questions.

Trap: Accumulating test counts or percentile screenshots without correcting the errors is activity, not evidence of improvement.

Phase I / objective

3. Learn what to leave, but do not hard-code an entire topic as untouchable

What the accessible sources report

  • His profile describes leaving difficult seating arrangements until later and learning attempt selection through mocks. Prashant Meena (written summary).
  • He describes choosing puzzle types he handled reliably and avoiding particular variants that consumed his time. Divyanshu (name as transcribed) at 30:40.
  • His profile emphasises accurate selection rather than attempting every question. Charugundla Sai Gireesh (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

Practise a first scan, solve the accessible questions first, and revisit longer sets only when the likely return justifies the time. Build skip decisions from your own timed performance and the actual question, not another candidate's dislike of a chapter.

Trap: Copying 'never do puzzles/input-output/critical reasoning' can discard an easy set. Conversely, an attractive set can become a time sink.

GA / ESI / FM

4. Turn scheme and report notes into questions with hidden answers

What the accessible sources report

  • He describes a two-sided scheme-note layout: prompts such as ministry, outlay, objectives and progress on one side, with answers covered during revision. Divyanshu (name as transcribed) at 37:00.
  • His profile separates descriptive evidence sheets from MCQ facts and explicitly uses closed-note active recall. S. B. Tanay Gaurav (written summary).
  • His profile describes short summary sheets and returning to recently studied material within a few days. Prasanth Akkiraju (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

After a topic, close the notes and reconstruct its definition, distinctions, mechanism and current linkage. For a scheme, recall ministry, target group, eligibility, benefit, implementation and dated update. For a report, recall publisher, edition, reference period, method, major finding and policy meaning. Check the original after retrieval.

Trap: Recognising a highlighted paragraph is not the same as producing the answer. Approximate recollection can help orientation, but exact-number MCQs still require exact verified figures.

Resources

5. Keep a stable core source; add a second source only to fill a named gap

What the accessible sources report

  • Her profile recommends limiting sources and repeatedly revising them. Shobhita Bhola (written summary).
  • His profile describes the need to filter a very large body of current-affairs notes using question relevance. Ankit Pandey (written summary).
  • He explains why he personally used multiple question sources after failures, and says resources provide tools rather than a selection guarantee. Divyanshu (name as transcribed) at 35:10.

How to apply it: our recommendation

Use a core chapter explanation plus your four existing collections. Merge new evidence into the same topic table. Add another source for a specific missing concept, disputed rule or shortage of suitable practice, not to restart the syllabus. Check high-stakes factual claims against primary documents.

Trap: Both extremes are risky: collecting ten overlapping magazines, or treating one coaching compilation as infallible. A provider-hosted interview is not independent proof that its paid product is necessary.

GA / ESI / Finance current affairs

6. Cover both news breadth and scheme/report depth

What the accessible sources report

  • He says his deep, Phase-II-oriented GA preparation did not fit a later paper that he experienced as more headline/one-liner oriented. Divyanshu (name as transcribed) at 13:50.
  • He describes preparing scheme details, relevant ministries and RBI notifications, with different lookback periods for different material. Divyanshu (name as transcribed) at 47:10.
  • His profile describes underestimating detailed objective questions and changing to daily objective practice with schemes and reports. Charugundla Sai Gireesh (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

Keep two layers: a broad factual scan for Phase I and a deep topic record for ESI/FM. Link one news event to its enduring concept, but also test names, dates, eligibility, targets, exceptions and institutional roles where relevant. Keep historical values distinct from operative updates.

Trap: Only analytical newspaper reading misses granular MCQs; only one-liners cannot support a descriptive mechanism or a multi-statement eligibility question.

Current-affairs planning

7. There is no verified universal 'exact number of months' rule

What the accessible sources report

  • His profile reports a three-month current-affairs choice under severe time pressure. Prashant Meena (written summary).
  • Her profile reports a four-month focus. Tejdeepthi Nimmakayala (written summary).
  • His profile reports a five-month focus. S. B. Tanay Gaurav (written summary).
  • He describes a short recent-news window for schemes alongside a longer window for RBI notifications. Divyanshu (name as transcribed) at 47:10.

How to apply it: our recommendation

Prioritise recent, relevant news while retaining older flagship schemes, recurring reports, foundational reforms and still-operative rules. Set depth and lookback by item type, syllabus and observed question demand. With a 2027 target, maintain a rolling update table now rather than gambling on a final crash window.

Trap: A successful candidate's time-constrained three/four/five-month choice is not an official boundary. Upload year is also not the selection year.

Whole preparation

8. Build Phase II before Phase I, then change emphasis rather than starting again

What the accessible sources report

  • Her profile recommends integrated preparation because the interval between stages is short. Shobhita Bhola (written summary).
  • His profile says he covered Phase II topics such as government schemes before Phase I. Utkarsh Agrawal (written summary).
  • Her profile describes losing a week after Phase I because she expected not to qualify. Bhavana P J (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

Before Phase I, build the FM/static ESI base, topic-linked current affairs and a minimum answer-writing habit. As Phase I approaches, increase timed gate-clearing practice. After the exam, take a planned recovery break if needed and resume Phase II rather than waiting for result speculation.

Trap: Waiting for Phase I results to begin FM or typing from zero leaves little recovery time. The opposite trap is preparing only Phase II and failing the Phase I gate.

Static ESI / Finance

9. Read first; use videos or AI to repair a specific conceptual gap

What the accessible sources report

  • He describes reading PDFs first, using other explanations for unclear concepts, making compact notes, and using PYQs to calibrate depth. Divyanshu (name as transcribed) at 40:50.
  • Her profile distinguishes easy topics read from notes from unfamiliar topics, such as balance sheets, studied through videos. Tejdeepthi Nimmakayala (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

For one chapter task, first try to explain it without help. Use your copyable AI prompt or a video for the exact point you cannot explain. Then solve an application or numerical question and revise the corrected explanation. Verify current facts and generated answers before adding them to your master notes.

Trap: Finishing all videos is not mastery. Equally, a polished AI answer can contain a wrong formula, fabricated rule or unsupported current figure.

Finance

10. Keep Finance numericals and static foundations; do not copy a successful gamble

What the accessible sources report

  • He explicitly says numericals could not be ignored and describes prior numerical practice and avoiding uncertain calculations in the exam. Divyanshu (name as transcribed) at 40:50.
  • His profile openly describes largely skipping hard-core Finance under time pressure and benefiting from the paper he encountered. Prashant Meena (written summary).
  • His profile describes leaning on Management while learning Finance basics because Finance was unfamiliar. S. B. Tanay Gaurav (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

Cover the numerical and accounting tasks already in your roadmap: state the formula, variables, units, assumptions, workings and interpretation. Practise fresh problems and distinguish a genuine content gap from a deliberate last-minute trade-off.

Trap: A favourable past paper does not make skipping Finance safe for 2027. Do not rely on the same Finance/Management choice mix recurring.

Management

11. Study Management as a case-diagnosis subject, not a name-theorist list

What the accessible sources report

  • His profile describes being surprised by case-based Management questions and recovering by starting with familiar questions. S. B. Tanay Gaurav (written summary).
  • His profile says he connected theories to college and workplace experience. Ankit Pandey (written summary).
  • His profile describes using workplace leadership and motivation examples rather than only generic textbook illustrations. Raghav Manglik (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

For each theory, learn its distinguishing conditions, closest competing model and a limitation. Diagnose a new case, identify the evidence supporting your choice, recommend a managerial action, and explain why the alternative theory fits less well.

Trap: Recognising Maslow/Herzberg on a chart does not prove you can distinguish them in an ambiguous case. A personal story without the theory's mechanism is also incomplete.

ESI / FM / English descriptive

12. Practise complete typed papers: knowledge must fit the clock

What the accessible sources report

  • His profile describes leaving substantial descriptive questions unanswered because of time management despite knowing the content. Utkarsh Agrawal (written summary).
  • Her profile describes a separate exam's typing problem and deliberately practising on a keyboard afterwards. Shobhita Bhola (written summary).
  • Her profile describes typing pressure and difficulty reaching her intended answer length in the exam hall. Tejdeepthi Nimmakayala (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

Type original answers under timed conditions, including planning, editing and moving between questions. Budget the session across all required answers using the applicable instructions. Assess demand coverage, accuracy, relevance and completion; measure usable output, not merely raw typing speed.

Trap: Reading model answers or drafting mentally does not test keyboard execution. Nor should a generic words-per-minute target override the actual paper instructions.

Descriptive writing

13. Answer the question's parts, not everything you know

What the accessible sources report

  • His profile says feedback taught him to answer the asked question point by point instead of reproducing all his knowledge. Satender Singh (written summary).
  • His profile describes concise theme notes combining an introduction, data, challenges, schemes and conclusion. S. B. Tanay Gaurav (written summary).
  • His profile describes theme-based evidence banks and a fixed answer framework. Raghav Manglik (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

Before typing, identify the command word, subparts, scope and required comparisons. Give each subpart visible space. Use only evidence that helps answer it. A compare/evaluate/diagnose question should not be forced into the same benefits-challenges-schemes template.

Trap: A rigid opening/body word split, exactly three advantages, or unrelated scheme names can crowd out the real demand. Interview accounts are not an official marking rubric.

English

14. Test precis, essay and RC separately before deciding English needs little work

What the accessible sources report

  • He singles out precis as requiring genuine comprehension and compression, and describes practice with feedback. Divyanshu (name as transcribed) at 45:12.
  • His profile says he spent less time on English because writing was already a strength, while still using a few mocks. S. B. Tanay Gaurav (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

Do one timed diagnostic of each task. For precis, preserve the central proposition and qualifications without importing outside facts. For an essay, address every dimension and sustain a coherent argument. For RC, answer from the passage when required. Re-practise the weakest operation.

Trap: Copying an already-fluent writer's low-practice routine is unsafe. Do not insert current-affairs facts into a passage-only answer just because they are relevant to its broad topic.

Revision / memorisation

15. Use a mind map as a retrieval index, not as the whole explanation

What the accessible sources report

  • His profile describes condensing FM chapters into a few pages and using mind maps for final revision. Prasanth Akkiraju (written summary).
  • Her profile describes mind maps as useful during compressed Phase II revision. Bhavana P J (written summary).
  • Her profile describes summary sheets and mind maps for quick revision after topic learning. Tejdeepthi Nimmakayala (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

Place the topic at the centre, then definition, mechanism, distinctions, application, current linkage and exception as branches. Reconstruct the map from memory. Put exact data, dates and units in a small companion table; keep the fuller explanation available for concepts the map cannot carry.

Trap: A beautiful infographic can hide missing logic. Colours and short labels do not establish understanding, factual accuracy or the ability to calculate.

Working aspirants / sustainability

16. Match tasks to your real schedule; do not imitate extreme routines

What the accessible sources report

  • His profile describes choosing night study rather than forcing an early-morning routine, and using short breaks for GA. Ankit Pandey (written summary).
  • His profile describes balancing demanding work with repeated revision of selected sources. Raghav Manglik (written summary).
  • Her profile describes leaving a job with family support; other reviewed profiles describe success while employed. Tejdeepthi Nimmakayala (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

Use short available slots for recall, MCQs and updating tables; reserve uninterrupted sessions for unfamiliar concepts and full typed practice. Plan breaks, sustainable sleep and a backup route. Decide employment changes using your own finances and obligations, not a success narrative.

Trap: Neither quitting work nor a 4 a.m. routine is a prerequisite. Do not copy sleep loss, workplace-rule violations or high-pressure life choices as study techniques.

Interview

17. Prepare your biodata and fundamentals, then leave time to act on feedback

What the accessible sources report

  • He describes receiving challenging feedback on fundamentals and spacing mock interviews to allow corrective study. Divyanshu (name as transcribed) at 52:30.
  • His profile describes preparation on RBI functions, annual reports, balance-sheet topics and peer mock sessions. Raghav Manglik (written summary).
  • His profile emphasises preparing claims in the biodata and admitting when an answer is not known. Utkarsh Agrawal (written summary).
  • His profile describes a previous mistake of treating the interview as easy after clearing the written stage. Satender Singh (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

Prepare truthful explanations of education, work, gaps, interests and certifications, plus RBI functions and relevant current issues. After each mock, repair the conceptual and communication gaps before another. Give a clear answer, distinguish uncertainty, and do not bluff.

Trap: Mock quantity does not substitute for feedback. Do not invent a hobby to steer questions or assume the panel will follow your preferred script.

Administrative / exam-day traps

18. Check eligibility and equipment before performance becomes irrelevant

What the accessible sources report

  • His written profile reports being stopped at document verification in an earlier attempt because of the qualification-date requirement. S. B. Tanay Gaurav (written summary).
  • His profile describes reporting a problematic keyboard during the descriptive exam. Satender Singh (written summary).

How to apply it: our recommendation

Read the applicable official notification for age, qualification completion/result date, category and documentary requirements. Keep supporting records ready. Follow centre instructions and promptly report a genuine equipment issue to the invigilator.

Trap: Clearing written cutoffs does not override eligibility. A person's account of a replacement keyboard or delayed start does not establish a right to extra time or permission to refuse to begin.

Conflicting advice: use a decision rule instead

Ask what prior preparation, time pressure and paper conditions made a candidate's choice possible. Do not turn a successful gamble into a general rule.

Advice that conflictsDifferences in the accountsSafer interpretation
Three vs four vs five months of newsPrashant, Tejdeepthi and Tanay report different windows; Divyanshu treats item types differently.Use a rolling, relevance-led update system. Keep recurring/operative older items. None of these windows is a guaranteed syllabus boundary.
One source vs multiple sourcesShobhita limits sources; Divyanshu uses additional practice sources after earlier failures.One stable learning spine, a controlled question bank, and primary-source verification. Add a resource only for an identified gap.
Skip Finance vs practise numericalsPrashant's profile reports a short-deadline gamble; Divyanshu says numerical practice matters.For a planned 2027 attempt, build Finance foundations and numerical competence. Do not generalise a lucky paper composition.
Write less well vs finish everythingPrasanth's and Tejdeepthi's profiles describe surviving incomplete/short answers; Utkarsh lost substantial answer opportunity.Aim for relevant, accurate answers across the required set within the clock. Neither padding nor deliberately leaving questions is the goal.
No dedicated English/typing work vs practise itTanay and Bhavana describe low practice in areas they felt able to manage; Shobhita deliberately trains typing and Divyanshu highlights precis.Use a timed diagnostic to decide the needed practice. Another candidate's pre-existing skill is not your baseline.
Resign vs prepare with a jobTejdeepthi's profile describes resigning with support; Ankit and Raghav describe studying while employed.This is a personal risk decision, not an exam rule. Sustainable time, finances and backup options matter.
Prepare only Phase-II-style GA vs broad headlinesSatender's profile advocates Phase-II-relevant GA; Divyanshu describes being hurt when the paper felt broader.Prioritise overlapping economic/social/banking news without eliminating the wider Phase I factual layer.

Apply this to your chapter tasks

The 480 prompts are a menu, not 480 notes-generation chores. Pick one task, obtain an explanation, verify it, retrieve it, then use it. Generating an answer is not evidence that you have learned it.

WhenSuggested action: our synthesisEvidence of completion
After each chapter taskClose the explanation; reconstruct a compact mind map. Answer a small set of fresh MCQs and one application question. Record what you could not recall.A checked retrieval attempt and an error entry, not simply a 'read' tick.
Each current-affairs updateCheck relevant items in CurrentAffairs-Monthly, Reports_NationalAndInternational, SchemesAndGovernmentPortals and StaticGK when supplied. Consolidate duplicates; verify important claims against the primary issuer.Topic, event, date, issuer, edition/reference period, figure/unit, rule status, source, static connection and last-checked date.
A regular descriptive slotType an answer to a syllabus/PYQ-style demand. Check every subpart, evidence relevance and timing. Use the actual word/time instructions of the practice paper.A completed answer plus a short correction list; do not measure success by length alone.
A weekly performance reviewReview sectional trends, recurring errors, retained topics and writing completion. Adjust next week's emphasis without abandoning stronger sections.Three specific repairs with a fresh-question retest; the cadence is our suggested workflow, not a topper consensus.
At intervals and near the examSimulate full sections and complete required descriptive sets. Practise moving on from difficult questions and check equipment/format familiarity.Evidence that your strategy works on unseen material under realistic constraints.

For ESI, pair a concept with a verified report or scheme application. For Finance, add a worked calculation or rule-application case. For Management, compare plausible theories in a fresh case. For English, type and review the actual task rather than only reading model responses.

Choose a chapter task and AI prompt

Traps in topper interviews themselves

  • Survivorship bias: candidates who made the same gamble and failed are missing.
  • Hidden starting advantage: three months of focused preparation may follow years of UPSC, banking, aptitude or writing practice.
  • Provider selection and editing: these sources are associated with one coaching publisher. Product praise is not an independent comparison or a purchase recommendation.
  • Recall and transcription error: scores, cutoffs, scheme figures and technical interview recollections are not verified official facts here.
  • Outcome does not validate every tactic: surviving little typing practice, a Finance omission or an incomplete paper does not make that tactic desirable.
  • Fixed-template trap: a successful framework is not a universal word split or official rubric.
  • Escalating commitment: persistence is not an instruction to sacrifice sleep, livelihood or all backup options indefinitely.

Detailed WHAT to study: evidence-linked inventories

This extension adds the distribution audit and concrete study demands to the original Phase II analysis below. It maps all 300 ESI/FM objective questions, all 60 descriptive options, all 20 essay options and all 10 precis/RC tasks in the supplied 2021-2025 sample. Prompts are paraphrased, not copied. The inventories explain preparation scope, not answer keys.

Distribution | ESI reports, schemes and policies | Finance and management | English task-by-task | Method and source limits

How to use: first read WHAT WAS ASKED; then study the named mechanisms/rules in WHAT TO PREPARE; finally complete the retrieval/application task. These are recommended depth targets, not future question predictions. Source references are optional verification: the study requirements are written here so you do not have to open PDFs to understand them.

Static, rules and current-affairs distribution

Verified counts, not invented objective marks. The 2021-2025 compilations contain 30 objective questions per ESI/FM paper but omit each question's weight. The recent structure is 50 objective plus 50 attempted descriptive marks. Question shares below are NOT measured mark shares. Descriptive choices offer 75 marks (three 15-mark and three 10-mark questions); the 50-mark attempt is two of each. Confirm the eventual exam rules from RBI.

Static = concepts, institutions and historical knowledge. Standing rules = scheme/product/ regulatory provisions, which may be old but need updating. Dated = report findings, events, incumbents, new initiatives or changed rules. A current passage can ask a static concept. Economics/social/environment boundaries are judgement calls; one primary label prevents double counting and the underlying CSV preserves overlap/source notes.

Reports

OECD Economic Outlook, March 2021 interim update

Observed in 1 distinct year(s): 2021. Year count describes this named theme, not a score allocation.

What was asked: Identify report/publisher; pandemic support finding; India's growth projection.

What to prepare: Record edition/date, publisher, forecast year, revision direction and policy rationale. Separate projected growth from realised growth and identify the denominator/reference period.

Depth / retrieval task: Make a report card with one projection, one finding and its economic explanation; update the edition rather than memorising the old forecast.

Evidence: 2021 OQ1 p73; 2021 OQ2 p73; 2021 OQ3 p73

Economic Survey 2020-21, 2023-24 and 2024-25

Observed in 3 distinct year(s): 2021, 2024, 2025. Year count describes this named theme, not a score allocation.

What was asked: Recovery explanation; Survey identification; agricultural production/growth; non-farm job requirement; MSME contribution and formalisation.

What to prepare: Study sectoral trends, growth drivers, employment estimates, agriculture, MSMEs and risks. Preserve financial year, averaging period, units, estimate/forecast status and source table.

Depth / retrieval task: Explain how a strong GDP number can coexist with employment problems; build a year-labelled sector indicator table.

Evidence: 2021 OQ19 p78; 2024 OQ9 p75; 2024 OQ10 p75; 2024 OQ11 p75; 2024 OQ12 p76; 2025 OQ14 p73

What to prepare: Know publisher, index versus project, survival/health/education dimensions, interpretation of score, country coverage and edition-specific rank. Rank, score and project membership are different facts.

Depth / retrieval task: Explain why improved income alone does not guarantee better human-capital outcomes.

English: detailed WHAT, not just topic labels

No fixed report/scheme reading list is established by English PYQs. Reports and ESI/FM knowledge can supply examples for essays; precis and RC must remain faithful to the given passage. Topic familiarity is not a substitute for reading and writing skills. The following are study/argument directions, not model essays or official marking rubrics.

All twenty offered essays: specific content and command

2021 option 1: Coding in schools

Primary preparation family: Education/learning. Essay: 40 marks; choose one of four.

What to prepare: Computational thinking, problem solving, creativity, teacher capacity, access, screen exposure and age-appropriate pedagogy.

Exact demand to practise: Weigh benefits and costs; distinguish coding literacy from compulsory early specialisation.

Output: Outline thesis, two benefits, two implementation risks, balanced curriculum and conclusion.

Evidence: 2021 English, physical PDF pp70-72.

2021 option 2: Future of Indian BPO

Primary preparation family: Business/digital. Essay: 40 marks; choose one of four.

What to prepare: Automation/AI, cost and skill advantages, higher-value services, data protection, global demand and reskilling.

Exact demand to practise: Analyse a future trajectory rather than narrating the industry's history.

Output: Build opportunity/threat/adaptation paragraphs with conditions for competitiveness.

Evidence: 2021 English, physical PDF pp70-72.

Primary preparation family: Business/digital. Essay: 40 marks; choose one of four.

Output: Use idea -> test -> implementation -> feedback; contrast innovation with novelty.

Precis and comprehension: all ten task records

2021 Precis: Sand scarcity and extraction

What to understand: Distinguish abundant sand from construction-suitable sand; retain demand, extraction, environmental damage and regulatory response.

Skill target: Preserve the causal chain; remove illustrative detail before dropping a main claim.

Constraint: Approximately 170 words in supplied paper.

Skill target: Do not turn may/could into will or add outside climate statistics.

Constraint: 180-200 words in supplied paper.

Evidence: 2025 English, physical PDF pp65-68.

2021 RC: Agorism passage / insurance questions mismatch

What to understand: The printed passage and subquestions do not match; use only for source-error recognition, not scored passage-based inference.

Skill target: Do not fabricate an insurance passage or answer with unrelated outside knowledge.

Constraint: 30 marks shown; content pair unusable for faithful RC marking.

Evidence: 2021 English, physical PDF pp70-72.

2022 RC: FMC-SEBI merger

What to understand: Retrieve reasons for integration, regulatory benefits, market-development implications and constraints from the passage.

Skill target: Distinguish what the author states from external knowledge of today's regulation.

Constraint: 30 marks; use own words and the actual question limits.

Five specific answer operations:

  1. Explain the original reason for commodity-market oversight.
  2. Explain expected effects of bringing FMC and SEBI together.
  3. Retrieve the historical rationale for separating commodities and securities.
  4. Trace the consequences of that institutional separation.
  5. Explain implications for exchanges and market participants.

Evidence: 2022 English, physical PDF pp65-69.

2023 RC: Inflation, business profits and distribution

What to understand: Track claims, supporting evidence, price/wage/profit relationships, competing explanations and qualifications.

Skill target: An economist's argument is not automatically the author's unconditional conclusion.

Constraint: 30 marks; answer the specific causal/comparative demand.

Five specific answer operations:

  1. Explain the proposed link between the cost-of-living crisis and business markups.
  2. Identify the conventional price-change measure used in the passage.
  3. Explain why CPI alone cannot allocate gains between workers and employers.
  4. Compare tax and profit contributions using the passage's stated period/evidence.
  5. Identify industries used as markup examples without generalising to every industry.

Evidence: 2023 English, physical PDF pp71-73.

2024 RC: Customer Relationship Management

What to understand: Explain functions, cross-team information flow, deployment choices, integration and implementation problems from the text.

Skill target: Separate a definition, a benefit, an implementation condition and an inference.

Constraint: 30 marks; unfamiliar business technology must remain passage-grounded.

Five specific answer operations:

  1. Explain CRM's principal function and business value.
  2. Trace how shared customer information supports cross-department collaboration.
  3. Compare cloud and on-premises deployment and the conditions favouring each.
  4. Diagnose data, integration, adoption and other implementation constraints in the text.
  5. Explain the described AI contribution without adding unsupported capabilities.

Evidence: 2024 English, physical PDF pp68-71.

2025 RC: Desalination, osmosis and power

What to understand: Track freshwater/saltwater flows, membrane/pressure mechanism, water-energy relationship and technical limitations.

Skill target: Draw a process diagram first; do not reverse the direction of flow or substitute general water-policy facts.

Constraint: 30 marks; preserve scientific relationships in plain language.

Five specific answer operations:

  1. Explain the local water problem and the desalination plant's role.
  2. Connect concentrated brine's environmental problem to the power-generation proposal.
  3. Explain membrane flow, pressure and electricity generation in the right causal order.
  4. Compare the stated advantages with other renewable sources.
  5. Identify expansion potential and the technological bottleneck specified in the text.

Evidence: 2025 English, physical PDF pp65-68.

The actual language syllabus to practise

Essay: decode command words, choose a defensible thesis, cover every requested dimension, organise causal/comparative paragraphs, provide relevant examples, test a counterargument and reach a reasoned conclusion. Practise direct introductions and precise transitions rather than memorised essays.

Precis: identify thesis and major propositions; preserve cause/contrast/qualification; generalise lists accurately; remove repetition/examples before central ideas; paraphrase, count words and check fidelity. Add a title only when required. An explicit word limit takes precedence over a mechanical one-third rule.

RC: distinguish retrieval, explanation, comparison and inference; match the answer to the command, use passage evidence, preserve technical relationships and paraphrase without changing meaning. External knowledge must not override the supplied text.

Language: subject-verb agreement, articles, tense consistency, pronoun reference, prepositions, parallel structure, punctuation, concise sentences and accurate vocabulary. Edit first for missing subparts/logic, then repetition, then grammar and word limit. These are recommended enabling skills, not a claim that grammar is a separate marked paper.

Reusable argument/evidence bank

Maintain five family sheets: climate/energy; business/digital; workplace/people; education/learning; social/health/philosophical. For each keep three mechanisms, two dated and verified examples, two counterarguments and practical implementation conditions. Use ESI climate/gender/welfare and FM digital-finance/management knowledge selectively; do not cram report names into an English essay simply to sound informed.

Evidence limits, coverage and update method

Every ESI/FM item has at least one inventory entry; an item can connect several themes. Consequently inventory theme/year counts overlap and must not be added as question totals. OQ means objective ordinal; DQ means descriptive option. Descriptive page references identify the verified section range, not a newly inferred exact question page.

2021 ESI OQ1 is printed Q11 by mistake; it is distinct from the real OQ11. 2021 ESI OQ5 lacks enough context for a reliable named-report attribution. 2025 ESI OQ11-14 follow a mismatched recreated agriculture passage; classification follows the actual MSME subquestions. The 2025 WDR welfare demand does not establish a precise edition. 2025 FM OQ28-30 explicitly warn that reconstructed question/theme may not be exact. Some regulatory preambles and thinker attributions are imprecise: authenticate rules and theories rather than learning recalled errors. 2021 English RC has incompatible passage/questions.

Update workflow: keep historical question evidence unchanged; add the latest verified edition/rule in a separate dated column. For a report record publisher, title/edition, reference period, method, three findings, policy implications and caveats. For a scheme record ministry/agency, objective, beneficiary, eligibility/exclusions, benefits/funding, delivery, current status and application cases. For policy record authority/instrument, old/new rule, effective date, applicability, rationale, mechanism, risks and exceptions.

Breadth safeguard: these inventories answer what the supplied papers asked; they do not replace the official syllabus. The original syllabus-wide analysis remains below. Suggested future reading or example programmes are not counted as historically named PYQs. No current legal limit, statistic, scheme availability or report finding is authenticated merely by its appearance in a memory-based question.

1. Evidence and the 75-80% score requirement

What was reviewed

Modern-format sample: all 150 objective prompts and 30 offered descriptive prompts in the five supplied 2021-2025 papers. Counts are questions offered, not attempts or marks. The 2019 ESI section is legacy objective-style evidence, not pooled with the modern mix. There is no supplied 2026 Phase II paper and no 2020 paper.

The real recurring pattern

Objective ESI often asks external knowledge around a passage, not comprehension from the passage alone. Reports, social programmes, benefit eligibility and regulatory overlap are prominent. Descriptive ESI demands explanation, evaluation, specific report/policy knowledge and multi-part coverage.

Breadth must protect descriptive choice

Social/demographic/gender/migration themes occur among descriptive choices in all five years. Climate/sustainability choices occur in four of five (2021, 2023-2025). Explicit monetary-policy descriptive prompts occur in three of five (2022, 2023, 2025). These overlapping theme observations are not exclusive chapter shares or forecasts.

Score engineering

Using the supplied guidebook's recent 50 objective + 50 descriptive structure: 40 net objective + 35 descriptive = 75; 43 + 37 = 80. With objective 40, reaching 80 requires 40/50 descriptive. A weak writing section cannot be assumed away. Confirm the actual 2027 structure, marking and choice rules from RBI.

Objective scoring must be mark-weighted

With quarter-mark penalty per question value: net = correct-mark value - 0.25 x wrong-mark value. Example: 18 correct two-mark + 7 correct one-mark questions = 43 positive marks; two wrong two-mark + two wrong one-mark questions deduct 1.5, giving 41.5/50 with one one-mark item left blank. Do not equate 80% of 30 questions with 40 marks.

The minimum breadth layer

Cover every supplied official syllabus heading at definition + mechanism + one example level. Then deepen recurring policy/report/beneficiary patterns. A high target is not compatible with treating the least frequent syllabus chapter as safely skippable.

2. Growth, poverty, jobs and sustainability: core depth

National income and measurement

Study GDP/GVA, nominal/real, deflator, per-capita income, growth versus development, stock/flow, base/reference period and limits of aggregate growth. Be able to interpret a simple indicator and explain why GDP growth need not improve employment or welfare. Stop before advanced national-accounting derivations and econometrics.

Poverty and welfare

Compare monetary and multidimensional poverty, incidence versus intensity, targeting errors, exclusion/inclusion, transfers versus public services and social protection. Depth test: explain a measure's merits and limitations, then connect a policy to an outcome. Evidence: 2021 descriptive Q2; 2023 Q4; 2025 Q1/Q3.

Employment and demographic transition

Study LFPR, WPR, unemployment definitions and survey reference periods; distinguish levels, participation, quality, informality, skills and underemployment. Explain female participation, youth jobs, MSMEs and labour-intensive growth. Evidence: 2021 Q5; 2022 Q4; 2023 Q6; 2024 Q1. Use latest comparable PLFS data, not mixed series.

Climate-growth mechanisms

Trace physical shocks -> farm output/food prices/health/productivity -> income, fiscal costs and financial risk. Distinguish mitigation/adaptation, intensity/absolute emissions, transition risk, green finance, just transition and SDGs. Evidence: 2021 Q6; 2023 Q3; 2024 Q3; 2025 Q3.

Exact depth needed

For each theme prepare: definition, causal chain, two or three distinct challenges, policy mechanisms, two dated evidence anchors, one implementation trade-off and a practical conclusion. Facts support an argument; they do not substitute for one.

What not to over-study

Avoid committee chronologies, advanced growth models, every poverty-line estimate, environmental treaty clauses and dozens of unverified figures. Retain the main measurement debates and current policy relevance; do not omit the underlying concepts.

3. Indian economy: the full breadth map

History, reforms, industrial and labour policy

Know the broad pre-/post-1991 transition: liberalisation, trade/financial opening, public/private roles, competition, disinvestment and labour-market formalisation. Prepare reform -> intended channel -> outcome/limitation. Evidence: 2021 DQ4, 2022 DQ2, 2024 DQ5; 2021 objective Q30 on labour-code objectives. Skip year-by-year historical narration unrelated to an argument.

Monetary and fiscal policy

Explain policy rates, liquidity tools, transmission, inflation targeting, lags and supply-side limits; tax/spending/borrowing, deficits, debt sustainability, fiscal multipliers and crowding in/out. Prepare coordinated and conflicting-policy cases. Evidence: 2021 objective Q14-17; 2022 DQ5; 2023 DQ5; 2025 DQ5.

Budget, Survey, public finance and political economy

Know BE/RE/actuals, revenue/capital, fiscal/revenue/primary deficit, transfers and federal finance. Read priorities and recommendations, not just allocations. Explain who benefits, financing and implementation incentives. Evidence: 2021 DQ1; 2024 objective Q9-13. Public finance includes Centre-state relations, not merely tax rates.

Agriculture, industry and services

Agriculture: productivity, water, market access, storage, diversification and price risk. Industry: MSME scale, credit, logistics, employment, corridors and competitiveness. Services: exports, digital/business services, jobs and unequal skill access. Use one sector map with bottleneck -> intervention -> trade-off; no crop encyclopaedia.

Money/financial markets, banks and RBI in development

Know the credit/intermediation channel, inclusion, NBFC-bank distinctions, savings, payment infrastructure and productive investment. Evidence: 2022 DQ3/Q6 and 2024 DQ6. ESI can cross into FM; narrow subject silos are unsafe.

Digital economy

Explain interoperability, access/usage, public digital rails, productivity, privacy, cyber risk and exclusion. Connect technology to outcomes and safeguards, not slogans. Evidence: 2024 DQ2/Q6 and 2025 objective MSME/formalisation cluster Q11-14.

4. Globalisation and social structure: do not leave gaps

Globalisation syllabus coverage

Study opening-up, trade creation/diversion, comparative advantage at an intuitive level, BoP/current-versus-financial flows, FDI/FPI, exchange-rate channels, reserves, WTO, IMF/World Bank, regional cooperation and contemporary fragmentation. Explain a global shock's path into India's inflation, trade, capital flows and growth.

Exact question forms

2021 DQ3 asks post-crisis globalisation, not a generic essay on trade. 2022 objective Q11-14 links a trade agreement to provisions/law; 2023 Q5-12 combines WTO facts and WEO/IMF knowledge. Learn mandate, framework and India application; skip every tariff line or treaty clause.

Demography, urbanisation and migration

Cover demographic dividend/ageing, jobs and human capital, rural-urban movement, housing, urban services, portability, remittances and migrant protection. Evidence: 2021 DQ5; 2023 DQ2; 2025 DQ4. Migration answers should consider both origin and destination and distinguish voluntary from distress migration.

Gender, social justice and multiculturalism

Cover unpaid care, safety, education/health, labour/asset access, discrimination, protective policy, participation and social cohesion. Multiculturalism is an explicit syllabus item, not disposable 'static sociology'. Evidence: 2022 DQ1; 2023 DQ1; 2024 DQ4; 2025 DQ2/Q6.

Breadth checkpoint

For each of the four official ESI headings, produce a closed-book concept map and a usable outline on an unseen subtopic. A recognised chapter title is not coverage. Use syllabus-based checks to compensate for the small five-year descriptive sample.

5. Objective ESI: scheme/report depth and linked sets

Three distinct tasks

Identify a scheme/report from context; recall facts not stated in the passage; apply rules to a person or case. Practise all three. A familiar passage does not mean its linked questions are answerable from the text.

Beneficiary and exception cases

Examples: PM-Kisan exclusions (2021 Q13; 2024 Q29), PM-KMY cases (2022 Q22; 2024 Q23), PM-JAY household coverage (2023 Q21), PMSBY accident/age cases (2025 Q1), adoption eligibility (2025 Q6). Learn boundaries, not only objectives.

Rules, components and operational detail

Examples: AMRUT Q6-10 in 2021; ONORC legal/delivery framework Q1-4 in 2022; women's savings Q30 in 2023; AIF eligible projects Q26 in 2024; PMAY-U 2.0 verticals/special groups Q25-26 in 2025. Major schemes sometimes require detail beyond a GA-level flashcard.

Report depth

World Bank Human Capital material (2022 Q15-17); WEO/IMF (2023 Q9-12); WDR middle-income-trap strategies (2024 Q5-8); Economic Survey sector/jobs material (2024 Q9-13); forests/report facts (2025 Q19/Q22). Prepare publisher, edition, framework, findings, India relevance and recommendations.

Boundary spillover

SGB/financial products recur in ESI (2021 Q24; 2022 Q21; 2023 Q24; 2024 Q30). The 2025 ESI compilation includes SIF Q10 and equity-derivatives/MWPL Q27-30. Treat these as observed cross-domain prompts, not grounds to relabel ESI as only schemes.

Two-level notes

Level 1 scheme card: ministry, objective, beneficiary/exclusion, benefit, funding, duration and latest change. Level 2 for selected major schemes: age/income/land thresholds, interactions with other benefits, components, delivery, withdrawal or grievance details as applicable. Add an eligible/ineligible mini-case.

Reports and schemes to prioritise

Latest applicable Budget/Survey, RBI Annual Report/RCF/FSR, World Bank WDR, IMF WEO, UNDP HDR, SDG/MPI, PLFS/NFHS and gender evidence; major jobs, agriculture, health, education, housing, pension, women/child and inclusion schemes. Read official summaries and relevant chapters selectively; update editions for the exam.

6. Descriptive ESI: turn knowledge into marks

Decode the demand before writing

Break a prompt into verb, topic, scope, named report/date and subparts. 'Evaluate' requires criteria and a judgement; 'discuss' requires a reasoned treatment; 'compare' needs common dimensions; 'explain' needs mechanisms. A report-specific prompt needs that report, not any relevant statistic.

A dependable answer architecture

Give a direct definition/context and thesis; organise the body to match subparts; explain mechanisms; use a few accurate evidence anchors; address implementation constraints/counterarguments; conclude with a prioritised way forward. Use headings where helpful, not a mechanical template that ignores the question.

Example: youth employment

Separate job availability from employability, participation and job quality. Connect skills mismatch, labour demand, MSME constraints and gender barriers to mechanisms. Match solutions to each constraint, name responsible actors and implementation conditions, and use comparable labour data. A scheme list alone is not analysis.

Evidence discipline

For each issue keep two or three reliable anchors: statistic + source/reference period, scheme/mechanism, and report recommendation or example. Never invent a rank, exact quotation or report finding. When an exact number is uncertain, make a defensible qualitative statement without pretending precision.

Self-review rubric - not RBI's marking scheme

Review demand coverage, conceptual accuracy, mechanism/analysis, relevant evidence, balance/feasibility and clarity/completion. Score each 0-2 for diagnosis, then rewrite the weakest part. This rubric does not convert reliably into official marks.

Time and word control

Under the recent 90-minute descriptive format, a starting budget is 5 minutes selection/planning, about 25 minutes for each 15-marker, 15 minutes for each 10-marker and 5 minutes review. Practise that mix in a keyboard interface. The recollections show 600/400-word labels; obey actual instructions, not a desire to pad.

Selection and readiness

Choose by all-subpart coverage and evidence, not topic familiarity alone. Keep enough breadth to have credible options among both mark bands. Judge readiness using fresh objective sets plus timed, externally reviewed writing; remembered PYQ outlines and generous self-scoring are weak evidence.

Studying with mind maps, tables and worked examples

Build small maps, not one giant subject map

Start with four branches: Growth and development; Indian economy; Globalisation; Social structure. Under each, list syllabus topics only. Create separate topic maps for poverty, employment, agriculture, migration, gender and monetary policy. Keep changing statistics in a separate evidence table.

Worked map: youth employment

Centre: YOUTH EMPLOYMENT. Measurement -> participation, employment, unemployment. Causes -> labour demand, skills mismatch, participation barriers. Consequences -> income insecurity, underused demographic potential. Responses -> enterprise/jobs, skills/apprenticeships, participation support. Constraints -> implementation capacity, access and job quality.

Label every important connection

Skills mismatch REDUCES employability; childcare availability CAN SUPPORT women's participation; enterprise growth CAN INCREASE labour demand. A line without a relationship label can hide weak understanding. Explain each arrow closed-book.

Evidence-table template

Columns: Claim | Indicator/example | Source and reference period | Limitation. Row 1: Gender participation gap | Comparable labour data | Relevant PLFS release | Participation is not job quality. Row 2: Skills matter | Skills/employment evidence | Verified report | Training alone does not create labour demand. Row 3: Enterprise can help | Programme mechanism | Official programme source | Credit alone may be insufficient.

Convert the map into a descriptive answer

For a youth-employment question: define the problem; select relevant causes; explain mechanisms; match causes to responses; add evidence and implementation constraints; conclude with priorities. The map stores knowledge, but the question determines the answer's structure. Do not reproduce every branch regardless of relevance.

Choose the right visual tool

Use causal chains for inflation, migration or climate effects; comparisons for poverty measures or policy alternatives; scheme tables for beneficiaries/exclusions; and answer outlines for evaluation. Each topic needs only the tools that serve it.

Making visual notes stick: recall and practice

Match the tool to the knowledge

Mind map: topic structure. Flowchart: how something works. Comparison table: similar items. Fact table/cards: values, dates and exceptions. Mini-case: application. Question-specific outline: descriptive writing. Error log: recurring mistakes.

Blank-page recall: the essential step

Close the source. Rebuild the map/table from memory. Explain the connections aloud. Compare with the source and correct missing/wrong elements. Attempt a fresh question. Recognising a finished map is not the same as knowing the topic.

Spaced retrieval

A practical starting schedule is next day -> one week -> two weeks -> one month, adjusted to recall. Hide table columns, reverse the prompt, vary the case and retrieve the relationship as well as the label. Update dated facts before reinforcing them.

A manageable 60-minute session

20 minutes: understand from existing notes. 10: make one small map/comparison table. 10: reconstruct closed-book. 15: apply through MCQs, a case or an answer outline. 5: record mistakes and the next review. For English, replace part of reading/organising with actual writing. Adapt the timings; do not make formatting the main activity.

The stopping rule

Every visual note must produce recalled facts, solved questions, explained cases or a written answer. If formatting takes more effort than testing, simplify. The goal is retrievable knowledge, not an attractive notebook.

How to interpret this audit

These are paraphrased offered prompts, not model answers or proof that the same topic will return. Recent papers list three 15-mark and three 10-mark options; use the actual selection instructions. Objective evidence references above are separate from descriptive Q numbers. DQ means descriptive question.

A 12-week integrated preparation path

Weeks 1-2: diagnose and establish breadth

Take fresh objective ESI/FM diagnostics and write one full English paper. Map every syllabus heading green/amber/red by closed-book performance, not reading completed. Establish core economics, financial-system basics and management theory cards. Start writing immediately, not after finishing all notes.

Weeks 3-5: deepen and connect

Work through ESI scheme/report cases, FM instruments/accounting/risk and applied management. Write timed answers on multiple syllabus areas; practise precis and RC weekly. Add current developments to existing static notes instead of building a second unrelated notebook.

Weeks 6-8: objective-to-descriptive transfer

Use mixed objective sets and choose answers from six-question descriptive menus. Test both mark bands and complete all English tasks. Repair stale facts, confused rules, weak mechanisms and incomplete subparts. Keep one current-affairs source.

Weeks 9-10: full-paper constraints

Run fresh timed papers with a keyboard and actual-style selection rules. Review mark-weighted objective net scores and externally reviewed writing separately. Do not hide one subject's weakness behind the aggregate.

Weeks 11-12: revision and verified updates

Prioritise retrieval, comparison sheets, short error logs and repeated timed completion. Update major reports/policies from applicable official releases. Limit new sources and stop expanding low-return detail.

Weekly outputs and readiness gate

Once foundations are established, work toward one fresh timed objective section and one full descriptive section each for ESI and FM, plus one full English paper per week. Review and rewrite before adding volume. Seek repeated objective performance around 40-43/50 net and independently reviewed complete answers around your planning targets; do not turn an unofficial review into a score guarantee. Track each subject separately across at least three fresh papers.

Protect Phase I work

If Phase I is only two months away, this is a parallel Phase II track, not a direction to abandon Phase I aptitude/GA. Start with one feasible Phase II content block and one short writing/recall block daily; increase after Phase I. Adapt time to your baseline and available hours.

Using your material without drowning in it

Assign each resource one job

Full notes explain; objective questions test discrimination; descriptive questions test organisation/application; short notes support retrieval; infographics refresh a map. Do not read all five versions cover-to-cover or make another full notebook.

Reverse-learning loop

Fresh question -> classify the gap -> targeted full-note repair -> short closed-book explanation -> a new application question -> spaced retest. Distinguish knowledge missing, rule confusion, stale value, weak analysis, poor selection and time failure.

One compact topic packet

Keep a concept map; one comparison table; a few dated evidence anchors; objective exceptions/rules; two descriptive skeletons; and your error list. One or two pages is a revision goal, not a restriction that forces important syllabus detail to disappear. Detailed notes remain the reference.

Currency and verification

Your Reports_NationalAndInternational, SchemesAndGovernmentPortals and CurrentAffairs-Monthly folders are useful starting material. File names/editions are not certification of current accuracy. Check official scope, release/reference date and policy effective date before using numbers in an exam.

English resource gap

No dedicated English folder appears under SubjectNotesForPhase2. Use the supplied usable English tasks and fresh passages for production practice; ESI/FM notes supply content, not a substitute for writing/precis feedback.

Evidence limits and official source stack

Authority

The official supplied syllabus is a 2025 Phase II excerpt. Exam timings, marks and choice structure used for planning are corroborated by the supplied guidebook pp26-27 and paper labels, not a supplied complete 2027 notification. Confirm final structure and instructions from RBI before the exam.

What the sample cannot establish

No candidate scripts, examiner rubrics, actual awarded descriptive marks or question-level empirical solve times were supplied. Therefore this guide cannot rank topics by proven scoring ease, promise 75-80, or infer exact future marks. Five modern papers support patterns, not a narrow guaranteed list.

Use historical questions correctly

Learn the concept/fact template, not stale figures. The guide paraphrases demands rather than endorsing every recollected premise. Automated old topic tags were not used as verified frequency counts. Offered prompt counts are not distinct concepts, candidate attempts or mark shares.

Official updates

RBI: https://www.rbi.org.in/ ; SEBI: https://www.sebi.gov.in/ ; Budget/Survey: https://www.indiabudget.gov.in/ ; MoSPI: https://mospi.gov.in/ ; PIB: https://pib.gov.in/ . Use the relevant ministry/report issuer for scheme eligibility and report-specific findings.
